# DeRay Mckesson, ACLU Urge Supreme Court to Defend Fundamental First Amendment Right to Protest


## Prominent civil rights activist asks court to reverse a Fifth Circuit ruling that vitiates First Amendment protections for millions of protesters


Case


:[Doe v. Mckesson (Ford v. Mckesson)](https://www.aclu.org/cases/doe-v-mckesson)


Affiliate

---

[ACLU of Louisiana](https://www.laaclu.org/)


Spokesperson


[Vera Eidelman › ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project](https://www.aclu.org/bios/vera-eidelman)


Media Contact


media@aclu.org(212) 549-2666

United States


WASHINGTON — The American Civil Liberties Union today asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review a lower court ruling that, if left standing, would gut First Amendment protections for the right to protest in the Fifth Circuit and potentially nationwide. The[petition for certiorari](https://www.aclu.org/cases/doe-v-mckesson?document=plaintiff-applicant-brief-certified-question) was filed on behalf of DeRay Mckesson, a prominent civil rights activist and Black Lives Matter movement organizer.


The case stems from a 2016 protest to celebrate the life of Alton Sterling, a Black Baton Rouge, Louisiana, resident who was shot and killed by two on-duty police officers. The plaintiff, a former police officer, was hit by a rock at the protest and argues that Mckesson, who was also present but did not throw the rock, should be liable for the injury. In 2024, a lower court granted summary judgment to Mckesson and found that the plaintiff failed to produce enough evidence to establish that Mckesson planned or controlled the protest or caused the officer’s injuries — and held that, regardless, opening him to liability without any evidence that he even intended the rock throwing would violate the First Amendment. In March 2026, the Fifth Circuit reversed that ruling.


“This lawsuit is designed to prevent people from standing together to fight for their rights. Unless the Supreme Court steps in, anyone could be sued for what someone else does at a protest, even something they never intended or wanted to happen,” said **DeRay Mckesson** . “The threat of an expensive lawsuit could scare people away from protesting at all.”


Since 2016, this case has been at the Fifth Circuit, the Louisiana Supreme Court, and the U.S. Supreme Court. Mckesson is asking the Supreme Court to resolve the question of whether the theory at its center — that protest organizers can be liable for the unlawful acts of a third party at a protest not because they intended the illegality but because they “negligently organized” the protest such that the illegality was foreseeable — violates the First Amendment.


“The right to protest is fundamental to American democracy,” said **Vera Eidelman, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project** . “But, if the Supreme Court doesn’t intervene, the First Amendment’s protection may lose much of its force. No one will be able to protest without having to fear the possibility of paying for someone else’s bad behavior that they couldn’t control and didn’t intend. That’s the definition of chilling.”


After the Fifth Circuit accepted the theory in 2023, the Supreme Court declined to again hear *Ford v. Mckesson* in April 2024. Despite the court’s denial of the cert petition, Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote a statement emphasizing the court’s 2023 decision in *Counterman v. Colorado* , which held that negligence is not the proper standard even when it comes to private threats, and that intent is necessary for political protest to be punished, should govern “any future proceedings in this case.”


“I am proud to represent DeRay Mckesson in this long fight and join him in urging the Supreme Court to overturn this profoundly mistaken decision,” said **David T. Goldberg of Donahue, Goldberg, Herzog & Davidson** . “The constitutional principles the Fifth Circuit discarded are fundamental, and the right at stake—to join with others to publicly demand accountability and justice—is a cornerstone of American self-government.”


After SCOTUS declined to review the case in 2024, it returned to district court, where Mckesson won summary judgment. Mckesson argued that the theory continues to violate the First Amendment and that, even if it is viable, Ford failed to meet his burden of proving the facts at the center of the case. The district court agreed. In March, the Fifth Circuit reversed that decision and opened the door for a jury trial of Mckesson to take place.


“It should shock every one of us that such a blatant attack on the First Amendment has made it this far in our courts,” said **Alanah Odoms, executive director of the ACLU of Louisiana.** “For 10 years, DeRay Mckesson has been made to answer for an act of violence someone else committed, simply because he attended a protest. If this nation truly reveres the Constitution as it claims to, this assault must fail. Once again, we are watching an attempt to force a retreat from rights guaranteed to every one of us.”


Mckesson is represented by David T. Goldberg of Donahue, Goldberg, Herzog & Davidson; David Cole; the American Civil Liberties Union; and the American Civil Liberties Union of Louisiana.


*Ford v. Mckesson* is a part of the ACLU’s[Joan and Irwin Jacobs Supreme Court Docket](https://www.aclu.org/defending-our-rights/court-battles/supreme-court) . You can read the petition for certiorari[here](https://www.aclu.org/cases/doe-v-mckesson?document=plaintiff-applicant-brief-certified-question) and more about the case[here](https://www.aclu.org/cases/doe-v-mckesson) .

### ACLU Releases Video of ICE Agent Slashing Observers’ Tire


PORTLAND – Two Portland-area residents filed an administrative complaint with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) today describing how ICE agents tailed and boxed them in with vehicles and slashed their car’s tire after they observed and filmed agents in a parking lot in Hillsboro, a suburb of Portland, Oregon. The video of the agents slashing the tire can be viewed here. The incident took place on October 7, 2026, amid a surge of ICE activity across the state of Oregon. The increase in ICE activity also coincided with a DHS social media post promising to target so-called “sanctuary” jurisdictions like Oregon. It is also the latest example of a pervasive pattern of retaliation against observers occurring all over the country; nationwide, federal agents have intimidated and harassed people observing and filming them in public, including by threatening them, tailing them, pulling them over without reasonable suspicion, surveilling their homes, and even assaulting and arresting them. “What happened to us is not unique, and that is what is so terrifying,” said A.P and M.P., ACLU clients. “We observe and record public ICE activity in order to shine a light on their abusive behavior and to create a record of what our government is up to. Because of that, they are terrorizing us and anyone else who dares to exercise their First Amendment right to hold our government accountable. We hope that sharing our story will bring attention to their reckless and unconstitutional attacks on our communities.” Over the past 18 months, the ACLU and its affiliates have brought several cases, including in Los Angeles, Chicago, and Minneapolis, representing observers who have been surveilled, intimidated, and harassed, for filming federal agents performing their duties in public. Most recently, the ACLU filed a case in Memphis, TN, where a federal task force has been terrorizing local communities for over a year and where observers describe a relentless retaliation campaign against them for filming task force agents. “The right to record publicly visible law enforcement activity is fundamental to our democracy,” said Scarlet Kim, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project. “Like many people across the country, our clients have been observing and recording ICE activity in their community. These videos have proven critical to exposing ICE’s abuses. If we cannot see and document what our own government is doing on our streets, we cannot hold it accountable for running roughshod over our rights.” “Masked federal officers have no business coming to Oregon to injure or intimidate people,” said Kelly Simon, legal director of the ACLU of Oregon. “Oregonians have the right to support their neighbors and communities by filming and documenting government abuses, and Oregonians should not have to fear retaliation when they exercise their right to record law enforcement.” The complaint demands that DHS investigate the incident, preserve all relevant evidence, and discipline the responsible agents. It further demands that DHS undertake a comprehensive investigation of the nationwide pattern of ICE agents retaliating against individuals observing and recording their activities. You can read the complaint here.

### CAIR and CAIR-Florida Urge Court to Temporarily Block Unconstitutional Terrorism Designation Before More Harm is Done


TALLAHASSEE — The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida heard arguments today in a lawsuit challenging Florida officials’ baseless and unconstitutional designation of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and its Florida chapter as “domestic terrorist organizations.” Unless the court intervenes to prevent it, the largest Muslim civil rights organization in the country will have to shut their doors in Florida on Nov. 5. “CAIR and CAIR-Florida are critical resources that people and institutions across Florida rely on to protect civil rights and liberties, and all we want to do is get back to that important work,” said Hiba Rahim, executive director of CAIR-FL. “Florida’s new law silences free speech, criminalizes association, and eradicates due process, and we are hopeful that the court will act to safeguard our constitutional rights. History reminds us that our country has endured dark chapters, but also that people who refused to accept injustice moved us closer to our founding ideals.” At today’s hearing, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) urged the court to grant emergency relief for the organizations, explaining the instant and debilitating harm CAIR and CAIR-FL will face if the court does not rescind the designation and stop it from going into effect. In the alternative, they are asking the court to prevent Florida state prosecutors from enforcing the law’s harsh criminal penalties against the nonprofits and third parties who associate with and support them. As the ACLU argued in court, CAIR and CAIR-Florida have done nothing to deserve this devastating designation. The state has never indicted, much less convicted, either CAIR or CAIR-Florida under any criminal law — and certainly not a criminal law involving the serious charge of terrorism. If the state tried to do so, it would fail. The reason is simple: Neither CAIR nor CAIR-Florida is engaged in terrorist activity, and the state would be unable to prove its case to a jury in a court of law. “Florida’s new law is an unprecedented abuse of state authority,” said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU’s National Security Project. “It gives state officials sweeping power to punish American organizations they brand as ‘terrorists,’ without due process and in violation of the First Amendment. We’re asking the court to block this unconstitutional law and ensure that our clients’ crucially important civil rights work serving Floridians is not silenced.” Once a designation becomes effective, an organization’s lawful, constitutionally protected speech and association are immediately rendered illegal and impossible. Under HB 1471, five Florida executive officials have the power to designate and debilitate U.S. groups — including nonprofits engaged in First Amendment-protected advocacy — without filing charges, initiating judicial proceedings, proving their case beyond a reasonable doubt, submitting the case to a jury, or complying with any of the other required constitutional protections of the criminal legal system. An elaborate set of prohibitions makes it a serious crime for the targeted American organization to do virtually anything in the state, and for others to work for or otherwise actively associate with or support the designated group. The consequences of violating these prohibitions are severe, including up to life imprisonment. “Florida’s designation of CAIR and CAIR-Florida flies in the face of fundamental rights guaranteed to all Americans by the Constitution,” said Scott McCoy, deputy legal director at SPLC. “All Floridians should be concerned that this law allows Florida officials to do an end run around the Constitution, shut down disfavored speech and advocacy, and impose draconian criminal penalties. If they are permitted to do it to these civil rights nonprofits, what’s to stop them from doing it to any Floridian with whom they disagree?” The impact on the Floridian communities CAIR and CAIR-Florida serve would also be immense. CAIR-Florida provides a range of pro bono legal services to Florida residents, including those who suﬀer government and workplace discrimination in violation of their civil rights, as well as those navigating the immigration system. “The state does not get to decide whose speech is constitutionally protected or whose due process rights deserve respect. The Constitution decided that long ago,” said Daniel Tilley, legal director of the ACLU of Florida. “And Florida must not strip CAIR and CAIR-FL of their ability to advocate and organize for the civil rights of Floridian Muslims. This dangerous designation regime, crafted by the DeSantis administration, seeks to criminalize protected speech, plain and simple — and with no regard for the harm it causes to the thousands of people our clients support and serve. We are proud to stand with our clients against this abuse of state power.” CAIR and CAIR-Florida are represented by the ACLU, ACLU of Florida, the Southern Poverty Law Center, and Bondurant Mixson & Elmore LLP.
